title: Mushroom Omelette
subtitle: Sautéed chestnut mushrooms folded into a soft French omelette
excerpt: Chestnut mushrooms cooked in butter until golden, then folded into a barely-set French omelette, a vegetarian breakfast that feels properly substantial without being heavy.
sourceNotes: A mushroom omelette is a standard filled omelette variation across French and British café cooking. Sautéing the mushrooms separately before folding them in is the standard technique.

glossaryTerms.definition: To cook food quickly in a small amount of fat over a high heat, moving or tossing it so it colours evenly and cooks through rapidly. From the French sauter, to jump. The high heat is what produces colour and concentrates flavour, a crowded pan lowers the temperature and steams instead.

content.text: A mushroom omelette has two short cooking stages run back to back. The mushrooms go first,

in butter until golden, then set aside while the omelette cooks in the same pan. Folding in the warm mushrooms at the last moment keeps the filling hot and stops the egg from overcooking. Chestnut mushrooms hold up better to the heat than button mushrooms and won't turn watery.

Heat the 20 cm frying pan over a high heat and add 10 g of the {{unsalted-butter}} butter. Once it foams and the foam begins to subside, add the {{mushrooms-chestnut}} sliced chestnut mushrooms in a single layer. Do not stir immediately, leave them for ninety seconds so they begin to colour on the underside. Then toss or stir and cook for another minute. Season with a pinch of {{sea-salt-flakes}} sea salt flakes and {{black-pepper}} black pepper, add half the {{chives}} chives, and tip the mushrooms onto a warm plate. Do not rinse the pan.
Why mushrooms must not be crowded

Mushrooms are mostly water. Crowd them in the pan and the temperature drops, the water steams out, and they boil rather than colour, you end up with pale, soft mushrooms sitting in their own liquid. For 100 g, a 20 cm pan is about right. If you are cooking for two and want double the mushrooms, use a larger pan or cook in two batches.

Beat the {{eggs}} eggs well and season lightly. Return the pan to medium-high heat, add the remaining 15 g of butter, and let it foam. Pour in the egg mixture and shake and draw with the spatula as you would for a plain omelette, the technique is identical. After twenty to twenty-five seconds the egg should be almost set. Scatter the warm mushrooms across the centre in a strip, then fold and roll the omelette onto a warm plate. Scatter the remaining chives over the top.

A mushroom omelette is a complete breakfast on its own. It goes well with buttered toast alongside to mop up any juices. For a more substantial plate, a handful of wilted spinach under the omelette adds something green and takes only a minute in the same pan with a splash of water before the mushrooms go in. The omelette does not keep, eat it the moment it hits the plate.

Mushrooms are pale and watery: the pan was not hot enough or they were packed too tightly. Start with a very hot pan and give them room to breathe, they need air circulation to brown rather than steam.

Omelette is overcooked by the time the mushrooms go in: the mushrooms cooled down too much before the omelette was ready, or the omelette cooking took too long. Keep the mushrooms on a warm plate and work quickly through the omelette stage.
